title: Exploring Count Regression
text:
2.1 Why not a linear model?









The function, DHARMa approximates new, predicted data from the fitted models and determining where the observed data is. If it was fitting the Gaussian model well, there would be uniform residuals along the QQ plot, however the shape notes that there is a cluster of low values near 0 and a cluster of higher values near 1. This linear model is not accurate predictive or representative of our count data. Deeper issues also lie, as Gaussian models can have negative counts with no bounds, however doctors visits in our data can’t be less than 0. It assumes a constant variance, however the variance grows with the mean, and Poisson predicts it is the same. Finally, it treats the effects as additive, however it’s more typical to multiply the count.

text:
2.5 Interpreting the combined table
The χ² value when looking between the null and a single predictor is 2175.43, with 1 df, and the p-value of < 0.001. When comparing the one predictor model to the full model, the χ² is 959.92, the df is 5, and the p-value is < 0.001.
The χ² statistic is the likelihood ratio, where the deviation will decrease with increased complexity as there are more factors as they account for more. The df accounts for how many parameters are being added, with the total number of variables being one more than the degrees of freedom. Finally, the p-value is the likelihood that that this is truly improvement if the simpler model were as good. We are going to be using he likelihood ratio value as a decision factor for the selected model, and the χ² value is 959.92 (p < 0.001), indicating significant improvement in fit. Therefore, our selected model is the Full Poisson model.
The provisionally selected model is Full, and the AIC value is 3.6596989^{4}, and the BIC value is 3.6641724^{4}.

title: Exploring Count Regression
text:
3.3 Interpreting the Diagnostics
The DHARMa plots suggest that the fit of the Poisson model is less than ideal. It can be seen that in both graphs, the values on the far left being the simulated values from the model are vastly different from the red line, being the actual values.
The dispersion ratio the plot has displayed is 7.25 (p < .001), and the expected rate of zero is 15.03 times the amount of zeros that the Poisson model expects, meaning that there is a greater variance in our data than the Poisson model can account for.
This overdispersion is important, as it carries the assumption that the variance is equal to the mean. Therefore, when this metric is incorrect, the other values that take into account the variance/mean, such as the standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-values, are also incorrect and likely decreased. We cannot, however move straight to a zero-inflated model after these results, as zeros can be generated from two processes: structural (individuals never visiting the physician office), or sampling (count process, where it’s sometimes zero).

Using a Likelihood Ratio Test to compare the Poisson model versus the negative binomial model, the χ² was found to be (1) = 1.212908^{4}, p < .001. These values show that the addition of another parameter (through the df value), as seen in the large Chisq value, showing that the model fits better the the added parameter. Additionally, both the AIC and BIC (3.6597^{4} to 2.447^{4}, 3.6642^{4} to 2.4521^{4} respectively) were significantly lowered. Through these values, we can conclude that the NB2 model is a better fit. This added parameter was valuable in allowing the variance to exceed the mean, however these values cannot yet illustrate other problems such as extreme counts and excess zeros.

title: Exploring Count Regression
text:
4.3 Double-Checking NB2 with DHARMa









We would like to perform additional tests regarding the dispersion, as it becomes close to zero it indicates non-significance. We would also like to observe whether the model has produced a number of zeros similar to the observed, determining whether a hurdle or zero-inflated model might be needed.
In double checking these plots, the QQ plots should (and are) closer to the diagonal line, in which they are, showing the NB2 is adequate with residuals being closer to predicted. However, the DHARMa residual vs predicted illustrates that there is a curve rather than the expected flat, fitted line. This curvature looks to have a pattern, meaning that the residuals likely are not random (as they should be, which would create the ideal straight line); this illustrated systemic changes, which are not desirable in a model, and they do not match the horizontal, red quantile lines.
















The negative binomial model has resolved overdispersion, as the ratio is now 1.04 (p = 0.432), and non-significant.

Visualizing Predicted Counts
Coefficients on the log scale are hard to picture, so it helps to plot what the model predicts on the count scale. Here we plot predicted article counts across mentor productivity, holding the other predictors at their reference levels (Men, Average) or means.









This model has created a curved line upwards, despite the predictors being linear, due to the use of a log link, as each year of school added isn’t 1, but rather the log of it, multiplying the expected count.

title: Exploring Count Regression
text:
6.7 Interpret the Interaction
Chronic Condition Association Differing by Gender? Throughout the tests performed, the LRT found was extremely small(χ²(1) = 0.01, p = 0.924), and upon adding the interaction, showing that adding the interaction did not increase predictive ability/fit. Furthermore, when incorporating AIC & BIC, the fit was worse (AIC = 2.44719^{4} vs. 2.44699^{4} without the interaction; BIC = 2.45294^{4} vs. 2.4521^{4}). Furthermore, in assessing the log contrasts between males and females, they are so similar that differences between them and interaction with chronic conditions cannot be deduced, and there are no differences in slopes. Generally, men have lower numbers of visits as a whole, whoever this is simply a gender difference, rather than reflective of the impact of less chronic conditions.
Confidence in the Interaction Using the omnibus results and probing tests, some data was revealed, however it did not necessarily increase the confidence in the interaction, as our data reflects a lack of interaction between chronic condition and gender. Using various tests, such as information criteria, the omnibus test as well as additional probing have not been reflective of moderated effects. While there are gender differences present, none of the tests have provided adequate values to assume anything beyond purely gender differences, for example, the gap with omnibus test are fairly constant and parallel, rather than intersection.

title: Exploring Count Regression
text:
7.2 Discussion
My results suggest that chronic conditions are seemingly have the strongest predictive abilities within the predictors. Realistically, this would be sensible, as those who have chronic conditions are likely seeking regular care measures and check-ins to ensure that their status hasn’t worsened they are not in pain, or that they are receiving a regimented treatment plan (Queenan et al., 2021). Self-perceived health is additionally important, as it will determine the frequency of visits in a purely subjective manner. That is one limitation of the study, is that ‘self-perceived health’ is a valuable measure, however it is more subjective and may be easily confounded by factors such as anxiety or hypochondriac symptomatology (Mobley et al., 2019). Those perceived in excellent health have less visits than those in poorer health, however the active choice to potentially ignore symptoms and self-identify as “healthy” may create a slight inaccuracy in the data. However, this metric is second most important in understanding what leads to physician office visits. Other variables such as insurance and education are slightly lower, and seemingly have less of an effect on visits, potentially as they do not directly relate to the health of an individual. Private insurance creates some effect, though, due to prevalent concerns and remains a barrier to treatment. Another limitation of this study could be the healthcare system in the region(s) that the study was performed. For instance, Ontario has the Ontario Health Insurance Plan, where regardless if they have private insurance, there are some treatments that would not require payments regardless, compared to the USA, where this is not the case (Ross University School of Medicine [RUSM], 2021). Gender was found to be generally insignificant, and other “life”-related factors seemingly took precedence - health issues can happen to anyone. The obvious limitations, other than the ones that were listed were additionally self-report measures which may additionally be skewed due to the subjective nature of surveys. With healthcare especially, there are additional barriers to consider such as: distance, accessibility, time, cost, limited appointment availability, etc (Canadian Institute for Health Information [CIHI], 2024).
